## Why This Matters

In L15 a single line did the magic: `loss.backward()` reached into a network of thousands of weights
and told each one which way to move. We took it on faith. This lesson removes the faith.
**Backpropagation is not a special neural-network trick -- it is the chain rule, applied
bookkeeping-style over a graph of operations, run once backward from the loss.** The fact that makes
deep learning possible: one reverse sweep computes the gradients for every parameter at a cost
comparable to the forward pass. Larger graphs still require more work; the saving is that backprop
does not run a separate forward pass for every weight. In the lab we build the whole engine in
about eighty lines (a faithful reproduction of Karpathy's *micrograd*) and watch it agree with PyTorch
to the last digit.

## Four Ways to a Derivative

| Method | How | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **By hand / symbolic** | differentiate the formula on paper | exact, but hopeless for millions of parameters |
| **Numerical** | `(f(x+h) - f(x-h)) / 2h` | easy, but one forward pass *per parameter* and imprecise -- a *check*, not a trainer |
| **Forward-mode autodiff** | propagate derivatives forward with the values | efficient for **few inputs, many outputs** |
| **Reverse-mode autodiff** | one forward pass, then one backward pass applying the chain rule | efficient for **many inputs, one output** -- the neural-net case |

A network has millions of inputs (the weights) and **one** output (the scalar loss). That is exactly
where **reverse-mode** wins, and it is what backprop uses.

## The Chain Rule and the Computational Graph

Everything rests on the **chain rule**: if `L` depends on `v`, and `v` depends on `u`, then

$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial u} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial v}\cdot\frac{\partial v}{\partial u}.$$

Write any expression as a **computational graph** -- a DAG whose nodes are the intermediate values
and whose edges are operations. Reverse-mode keeps, for each node, the quantity $\partial L/\partial
v$ (its **grad**), and pushes it to the node's inputs by multiplying by the **local derivative**
$\partial v/\partial u$ -- a quantity each operation knows about itself (for `a*b`, the local
derivatives are simply `b` and `a`).

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  a["a = 2"] --> e["e = a*b = -6"]
  b["b = -3"] --> e
  e --> d["d = e + c = 4"]
  c["c = 10"] --> d
  d --> L["L = d*f = -8"]
  f["f = -2"] --> L
```

That is the graph for `L = (a*b + c)*f`. The forward pass fills in the values left to right; the
backward pass seeds $\partial L/\partial L = 1$ at the right and flows gradients back to the left,
landing on $\partial L/\partial a = 6$, $\partial L/\partial b = -4$, and so on -- which the lab
confirms by hand, against PyTorch, and numerically.

## Reverse-Mode in Three Moves

1. **Forward pass.** Compute every node's value and remember the graph (who produced whom, and each
   node's local-derivative rule).
2. **Topological order.** Sort nodes so each comes after everything it depends on. A node's gradient
   is only correct once *all* the nodes it feeds have pushed their share -- reverse topological order
   guarantees that.
3. **Backward sweep.** Seed $\partial L/\partial L = 1$, then walk the graph in reverse, each node
   adding its contribution into its inputs' grads via the local derivative.

::: {.callout-important title="Gradients accumulate"}
Every gradient push uses `+=`, not `=`. If a node feeds into several places, its gradient is the
**sum** of the contributions from each path (the multivariable chain rule). That is also why a
training loop must call `zero_grad()` every step: otherwise this step's gradients pile on top of last
step's. The `optimizer.zero_grad()` from L15 is exactly this reset.
:::

## Backprop = Reverse-Mode Autodiff on the Loss

Put it together: **backpropagation is reverse-mode autodiff with the loss as the output.** One
forward pass to compute the loss, one backward pass to get the gradient of that loss with respect to
every parameter. The backward pass is typically a constant-factor multiple of the forward pass: both
costs grow with the operations and parameters in the graph, but reverse-mode obtains all parameter
gradients in one sweep instead of re-running the model once per parameter. That distinction is why
training networks with millions (or billions) of weights is feasible.

## PyTorch `autograd` Is the Same Engine

PyTorch's `autograd` is precisely the engine you build in the lab, with two differences: its nodes
are **tensors** (one operation differentiates a whole matrix at once), and it is written in C++/CUDA
for speed. Everything else is identical -- a dynamic graph, a `.backward()` that walks it in reverse,
and gradients that **accumulate** in `.grad`:

```python
x = torch.tensor([2.0, 0.0])
w = torch.tensor([-3.0, 1.0], requires_grad=True)
b = torch.tensor(6.8813735870195432, requires_grad=True)
o = torch.tanh((x * w).sum() + b)
o.backward()        # fills w.grad and b.grad -- same numbers as our scalar engine
```

Mark a tensor with `requires_grad=True`, build an expression, call `.backward()` on the final scalar,
and read each input's `.grad`. (You can also get gradients without populating `.grad` via
`torch.autograd.grad`.) When you wrote `loss.backward()` in L15, *this* is what ran.

## Common Pitfalls

- **Forgetting gradients accumulate.** Without `zero_grad()` each step, gradients from previous steps
  pile up and training goes haywire. The `+=` in the engine is the reason.
- **Confusing numerical with autodiff.** Finite differences are a great *check*, but they need a
  forward pass per parameter and lose precision -- useless for training. Backprop is exact and cheap.
- **Thinking backprop is neural-network-specific.** It is general reverse-mode autodiff; it
  differentiates any computational graph, not just nets.
- **Mixing up the modes.** Reverse-mode is for many-inputs/one-output (nets); forward-mode is the
  opposite. Using the wrong one is asymptotically slow.

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"Is backprop just the chain rule?"** -- Essentially yes, plus the bookkeeping that makes it
efficient: storing each intermediate value, knowing each operation's local derivative, and sweeping
the graph once in reverse topological order so no gradient is computed twice. The insight is not the
calculus; it is the *one backward pass* organization.

**"Why not just use numerical gradients?"** -- They are simple and great for *checking* a gradient,
but training needs the gradient with respect to every parameter, and finite differences cost a
forward pass *each* -- millions of forward passes per step -- and lose precision. Backprop delivers
all of them exactly in a single backward pass.

**"Do I ever write `.backward()` myself?"** -- Almost never; you call PyTorch's. But understanding it
demystifies the bugs you *will* hit: a gradient that is `None` (you forgot `requires_grad`, or
detached the graph), gradients that explode because you forgot `zero_grad`, or "backward through the
graph a second time" errors. The black box becomes debuggable.

## Summary / Cheat-sheet

| Concept | The one-liner |
|---|---|
| Backpropagation | reverse-mode autodiff applied to the loss: one forward pass, one backward pass |
| Chain rule | `dL/du = (dL/dv)(dv/du)` -- compose local derivatives along the graph |
| Computational graph | the DAG of operations; each node remembers how it was made |
| Local derivative | each operation's own derivative (for `a*b`: `b` and `a`) |
| Reverse topological order | process nodes so each grad is complete before it pushes |
| Gradients accumulate | `+=` where a node fans out -- hence `zero_grad()` each step |
| Cost | one backward sweep gets all parameter gradients; its work is comparable to a forward pass and scales with the graph |
| PyTorch autograd | the same engine, vectorized over tensors -- `requires_grad`, `.backward()`, `.grad` |
